## Evaluation designs{.smaller}

- Experimental   
  - Randomized controlled trial

- Quasi-experimental   
  - Instrumental variable (IV)
  - Regression discontinuity (RDD)
  - Difference in differences (DiD)

- Observational (Non-experimental)  
  - Time–series analysis (Pre- and post-intervention studies)
  - Cross-sectional surveys
  - Case studies


## Case Study vs. Quantitative Impact Evaluation

:::{style="font-size:20px;"}
| Dimension | Quantitative Impact Evaluation | Qualitative Case Study |
|:--|:---|:---|
| Main questions | Does it work? How much? | How and why does it work? |
| Primary focus | Causal effects and outcomes | Processes, mechanisms, context |
| Typical methods | RCT, RDD, DiD, IV | Interviews, observations, documents |
| Data | Numerical, structured | Textual, observational, documentary |
| Strengths | Estimates program impacts | Explains implementation and experiences |
| Limitations | May not explain mechanisms | Limited statistical generalization |
:::

:::{style="font-size:24px;"}
**Key takeaway:** Quantitative methods estimate program impacts; qualitative case studies help explain how and why those impacts occur.
:::



## Case study questions

:::{style="font-size:24px;"}
| Item                   | Assignment                                                    |
| :--------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Exercise| Suppose you are working for GAO and have been asked whether the informed consent requirements for experimentation with human subjects are being properly implemented. Suppose further that we visit three sites where humans are used as subjects for research— a hospital, a university, and a clinic— and that we review the informed consent procedures at each site.   |
| Question 1         | Is this an application of the case study method? Why?    |
| Question 2          | If not, would case studies be appropriate for answering the question we were asked? Why? |
| Question 3          | What is your definition of “case study”? |
:::

:::footer
Source: Adapted from GAO, [Case Study Evaluations](https://www.gao.gov/assets/pemd-10.1.9.pdf)
:::

## What is a case study?

>A case study is a method for learning about a complex instance, based on a comprehensive understanding of that instance obtained by extensive description and analysis of that instance taken as a whole and in its context.

:::footer
Source: GAO, [Case Study Evaluations](https://www.gao.gov/assets/pemd-10.1.9.pdf)
:::


## Case study

- The "Why" and "How" questions
- Exam program implementation
- Program must adapt to organizational context and local conditions

:::footer
Source: @newcomer_handbook_2015
:::


## Categories

::: {style="font-size:32px;"}
- Illustrative: descriptive, add realism and in-depth examples
- Exploratory: descriptive, defining the questions and hypotheses for later investigation
- Critical instance: critical test of an assertion about program, problem or strategy
- Program implementation: operation and norms about implementation
- Program effects: cause-and-effect relationships, involve multiple sites and multiple methods
- Cumulative: brings together findings from many case studies
:::

:::footer
Source: @newcomer_handbook_2015, GAO, [Case Study Evaluations](https://www.gao.gov/assets/pemd-10.1.9.pdf)
:::


## Steps in case studies

:::{style="font-size:20px;"}
- Designing the Case Study. 
  - Define the research questions.  
  - Develop a framework to identify study dimensions.  
  - Determine the unit of analysis.  
  - Establish a single-case or multiple-case design.  

- Conducting the Case Study. 
  - Develop protocols.  
  - Select qualified staff and provide training.  
  - Implement strategies for collecting data, typically from multiple sources.  

- Analyzing the Data. 
  - Create a database.
  - Use specific techniques to analyze the data.  

- Preparing the Report. 
  - Determine the audience and the organizational structure for the report.  
  - Include context and data collection strategies in addition to findings.  
  - Outline limitations or cautions.  
:::

:::footer
Source: @newcomer_handbook_2015
:::



## Common Data Collection Methods

::: {style="font-size:30px;"}
- **Interviews:** Understand individual experiences and perspectives

- **Focus groups:** Explore shared experiences and differences

- **Observations:** Examine how programs operate in practice

- **Document analysis:** Review policies, reports, and administrative records

- **Surveys:** Collect structured information from participants
:::


## Triangulation: Strengthening Evidence

::: {style="font-size:30px;"}

**Compare findings across multiple sources and methods.**

Example: Why is participation in a workforce program declining?

- Interviews → Participants report transportation barriers

- Administrative data → Attendance is lower in distant neighborhoods

- Observations → Limited transportation options near program sites

**Converging evidence strengthens the explanation.**
:::

## Case Study Exercise: NYC Gifted and Talented Program

::: {style="font-size:30px;"}
**Scenario:** NYC wants to evaluate the implementation, accessibility, and effectiveness of its Gifted and Talented (G&T) Program.
:::

#### Group Discussion (10 minutes)

::: {style="font-size:24px;"}
| Topics | Evaluation Focus | Research Question |
|:-|:--|:-----|
| 1 | Access and Equity | What factors influence whether families apply? |
| 2 | Implementation | How do schools differ in implementing G&T? |
| 3 | Stakeholder Perspectives | How do parents and teachers define success? |
| 4 | Program Improvement | What changes could improve accessibility? |
:::


## Designing case study

- Define the research questions
- Develop a framework to identify study dimensions
- Determine the unit of analysis
- Establish a single-case or multiple-case design
- Select cases or sites


## Avoiding common pitfalls

:::{style="font-size:24px;"}
| Problem                | Solution                                                                       |
| :--------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------- |
| Limited generalization | Sites selection </br> Acknowledge limitation                                   |
| Too much data          | Research framework  </br> Protocols                                            |
| Impartiality           | Review interview </br> Multiple data collection </br> Supervision and training |
| Premature conclusions  | Multiple data analysis </br> Rival hypotheses                                  |
| Narrative bias         | Understand audience </br> Explicit interpretation                              |
:::
